A whole training session, step by step

Before the session, take five minutes with the coach. Agree on a pause sign and learn his hand signals. Ask which lead method he teaches (how he wants the shooter to get in front of the target) and which words he uses for lead. Then the group gathers for the safety briefing: interpret it consecutively, sentence by sentence, firmly and completely.

On the first stand the coach usually starts without cartridges: an eye-dominance check, then the stance and the ready position. In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ the gun starts low, below the line on the vest; in Compak® Sporting the gun position at the call is free. Whisper his corrections from behind (chuchotage) while he moves feet and hands.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 3 · Ready position: feet and gun

Next comes reading the target. The coach shows it, asks where the shooter first sees it clearly, and sets the pick-up point, the hold point and the break point. Use the same three words in your language all day, so the guest learns them.

Now the shooting. Between targets the coach gives cues of two to five words. You repeat them, as short as the coach said them and in the same order, while the gun is open. When the coach names the cause of a miss, such as “behind”, “over the top” or “you stopped”, translate it together with the fix. The shooter needs both: what went wrong and what to change. Pass on praise with the same energy.

Then the pairs: which target comes first, “eyes first, then the gun”, and the second shot of the double. Finally the debrief, consecutive again, where the coach sums up two or three points. Write them down in both languages and give the guest the note. Below is a typical chain of phrases in the order you are likely to hear them.

Tip: If the guest competes the next day, remind everyone that coaching is forbidden during the competition. The coach cannot advise, and you interpret only for the referee, the jury and the organiser. More in Your role: training versus competition.

Key points

  • Before: pause sign, lead method, lead words, hand signals
  • Safety briefing: consecutive, firm, complete
  • Same three terms all day: pick-up, hold, break point
  • Cues between targets: same length, gun open; cause + fix together
  • Debrief: write the key points in both languages
Stand Talk

  • Coach Morning, everyone. Before we load anything, a quick safety briefing.

    Meaning: Start of the session; interpret the briefing consecutively and completely.

  • Coach Guns stay open until you’re on the stand and I say “load”.

    Meaning: No closed guns off the stand; loading only on the coach’s word.

  • Coach Point at my nose, both eyes open. Now close your left eye.

    Meaning: Eye-dominance check: if the finger jumps, the right eye is not the master eye.

  • Coach Front foot pointing at the break point, weight forward.

    Meaning: Stance: set the feet for where the target will be broken; lean slightly forward.

  • Coach Gun down, stock under the line. Mount only when you see it.

    Meaning: Sporting™ ready position: the mount starts only after the target appears; in Compak® Sporting the position at the call is free.

  • Coach Watch this one. Where do you first see it clearly?

    Meaning: The coach is setting the pick-up point.

  • Coach Hold your muzzles about halfway back, just under the line.

    Meaning: Hold point between pick-up and break point, slightly below the target’s path.

  • Coach Behind it. Give it more.

    Meaning: The shot passed behind the target: more lead.

  • Coach Call it three feet — that’s the picture you want.

    Meaning: The gap the coach wants the shooter to see at the shot. “Three feet” describes how it looks, not a measured distance, so keep the unit.

  • Coach Over the top. You lifted your head — stay in the gun.

    Meaning: Miss above, caused by the cheek leaving the stock (head lift).

  • Coach Smoked it! Same again.

    Meaning: Perfect hit; repeat exactly what you did.

  • Coach You stopped the gun. Keep it moving through the shot.

    Meaning: Miss behind because the swing stopped (stopping the gun); follow through.

  • Coach Next is a report pair: crosser first, then the rabbit.

    Meaning: A double on report: the rabbit is released by the sound of the shot at the crosser.

  • Coach Eyes first, then the gun.

    Meaning: On the second target, find it with the eyes before moving the muzzles.

  • Coach Keep the muzzles under the rabbit.

    Meaning: Keep the muzzles below the rabbit: if it bounces up, it hops into the shot instead of over it.

  • Coach Change to quarter and half for this stand.

    Meaning: Fit 1/4 and 1/2 chokes (open, then a little tighter).

  • Coach Let’s call it a day. Three things for tomorrow: feet, head, follow-through.

    Meaning: End of session; the coach sums up — write these down for the guest.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. When is the safety briefing interpreted, and how?

    1. Briefly, in a whisper, while they load
    2. At the start, consecutively and in full
    3. Only if one of the guests asks for it
    4. After the first stand, in a summary
    Answer

    At the start, consecutively and in full

    Safety comes first and must not be shortened; consecutive mode lets each rule land.

  2. The coach says “Behind it. Give it more.” Which rendering between targets is right?

    1. Two short parts: “behind”, “more lead”
    2. A longer, gentler sentence with tips
    3. Only the fix: “shoot a bit earlier”
    4. Only praise: “good, same again”
    Answer

    Two short parts: “behind”, “more lead”

    Follow the coach: same length, same order, what went wrong plus what to change, nothing added.

  3. Why keep the same words for “pick-up point”, “hold point” and “break point” all day?

    1. The rules require these exact words
    2. So the coach can follow your language
    3. So the guest learns three clear ideas
    4. It does not matter which words you use
    Answer

    So the guest learns three clear ideas

    Using the same words each time helps the guest learn the three ideas; if you change the words, three ideas look like six.
